I’m a Glass. I like transparency.

So here’s what you’ll see when you tap “Pricing & Fees” in the Olo App.

The restaurant sets the menu price.
It’s the same price you’d see in store or on the brand’s own app.

Our 5% Network Fee is what we collect to host this multi-brand app experience.
We call it out by name.

And we tell you how to skip it: order directly from the brand.

That’s not a flaw in our business model.
It’s our business model.
Olo powers restaurants’ own digital channels, and that’s where guests get the best price.

Tips go 100% to the party named in the tip description.

Delivery fees sit on their own line, so you can see exactly what you’d save by switching to pickup.

Why does this matter?

Most multi-brand apps charge restaurants a commission.
To cover it, menu prices on those apps often run 15% to 30% higher than in store.

We commissioned a study on this.
Most guests expect delivery fees.
Only 27% of American adults know about menu markups.
That means 73% have no idea they’re paying them.

Entrepreneur Media covered the findings yesterday (link in the first comment).

Restaurants haven’t suddenly gotten really expensive.
The markup has been hiding in plain sight.

Transparent pricing has been missing from multi-brand restaurant apps until now.
We’re thrilled to change that.

Olo is always on the restaurant’s side.
And honest with their guests, too.

Did you know about menu markups on multi-brand apps?

AI Telco Shorts Episode #2 | Perspectives from Asia with Dr. Rainer Deutschmann, Chief Strategy & Transformation Officer, Axiata Group.

My key takeaway: Telcos are the ultimate AI laboratories, sitting on billions of real-world transactions, customer interactions, and network events that generate insights no one else can replicate.

AI is compounding at an extraordinary rate, with hardware capability, AI investment and algorithmic breakthroughs...all growing exponentially.

So what should telcos do now?

1️⃣ Define 'where you play'
Everyone can buy a model. Focus on what you have earned, not what anyone can buy. Telcos' competitive advantage lies in their data, customer relationships, trust, and ability to learn faster than the competition.

2️⃣ Redefine 'how you run'
Build a self-learning organisation. Simplify before you automate, automate before you agentify, and embed AI into the fabric of business processes.

3️⃣ Decide 'where humans sit'
As AI takes on more tasks, the role of humans increasingly becomes that of directors, evaluators, and boundary-setters...steering the organisation, judging outcomes, and intervening when exceptions demand it.

Watch episode two and share your perspective: which of these actions are most urgent for telcos today, and where is the industry still falling behind?

Space, Telecom & AI - A New Era of Connectivity !

The strategic question is not simply how telcos respond to SpaceX, but how they position themselves to lead in a world where connectivity is increasingly ubiquitous and AI drives differentiation.

posts.content:
My Weekly Telecom Technology View
26 October 2026

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜-𝗥𝗔𝗡 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆 𝗶𝘁.

I’m encouraged by the engineering progress. I’m less convinced by the assumption that putting AI compute into a network automatically creates a business.

This week’s T-Mobile AI-RAN call and Elisa’s trial combining radio and AI workloads move technical feasibility forward. AT&T’s separate AI networking MVP explores another part of the problem: controlling how applications reach models, handle data and consume budget.

There is a bigger telecom story here. The location of computing is becoming part of the service decision.

An industrial application may need inference near a machine. A consumer assistant may keep sensitive processing on the device. Other workloads will run more economically in a central cloud. The operator’s opportunity is to make those choices work together without asking customers to manage the boundaries.

That could change what telcos sell, how they design networks and how they support customers. But first, we need to separate two investment cases: AI that improves radio performance, and AI applications that share network computing resources. 𝗔 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿.

Shared infrastructure introduces a practical tension. Radio processing has deadlines; AI demand can be unpredictable. Protecting connectivity may leave compute idle. Selling that capacity too aggressively could compromise the service customers already pay for.

The commercial design therefore belongs in the architecture discussion. What capacity can be committed? Who pays for reservations? Can the application move elsewhere? Does the price cover power, software, support and partner margins?

I would insist on those answers before approving a wider rollout.

Over time, I see a credible role for telcos in operating distributed AI services. Their reach matters, but the advantage must be earned through reliable delivery, customer access and disciplined economics. Hyperscalers and application providers will remain formidable partners and competitors.

𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗳𝘆 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁?

HCLTech’s network engineering, AI infrastructure and managed operations capabilities are relevant here: helping operators test the architecture and operating model together before committing at scale.

Third post in the Oleshky series and part 2 of Stuart Ramsay’s Sky News reporting from the frontlines.  See link below.
A week must have felt like a lifetime for the two Ukrainian women who escaped from occupied Oleshky, now known globally as the town where Russian soldiers are using civilians as a human shield. 
Here, Stuart speaks with the women and with Kseniia Arhipova, a Ukrainian police detective who is relentlessly enabling escapes.
A tentative ceasefire, allegedly led by the Pope and Melania Trump, is underway to make space for the inload of food and to prepare the way for a planned evacuation of Ukrainians wanting to leave from 29 Oct.
There is much scepticism with claims of a convenient pre-mid-terms PR stunt for Trump and leverage for Putin. A short-term gain.
Regardless, this winter will likely be the worst yet for civilians in this war.  A chance to save a few from starvation and freezing to death should not be sniffed at.  Trump will claim glory no matter what.
I just hope it is possible to implement robust control and constant public monitoring over where the evacuated people end up. Evacuation must be transparent and to safe destinations.
The relief on the faces of the two female escapees is enough to send a message that an evacuation will be welcome for some.  In a saturated online pit of disinformation, it is important that Ukrainians know that they are not being forgotten by the wider world.  It is important that the Ukrainian soldiers who are tasked to monitor these places 24/7, seeking random opportunities to save lives, know that we are supporting them.  The mental toll on them is enormous. People are doing good work here and we should back them.

How many customers are restaurants losing before they even place an order?

Think about the last time you ordered food online.

How many steps did it take to find the menu, customize your order, and check out?

For restaurants, having an online ordering system is only part of the equation. Making it easy for customers to actually use it is what matters.

A few things can make a big difference:

- A clear "Order Online" button that's easy to find.
- A simple menu that's easy to navigate.
- A checkout process that doesn't require unnecessary steps.
- An ordering experience that works just as well on a phone as it does on a computer.

Restaurants invest time and money into bringing customers through their doors. Their digital experience deserves that same attention.

Sometimes, improving online ordering isn't about adding more features. It's about removing friction.

signals.text: Naming the fee is the easy half. The harder question for an operator is attribution: 5% on a guest who was already ordering direct is a cost, while 5% on a genuinely new guest is cheap acquisition. Since the guest data comes back to the brand, will operators be able to see which Olo App orders came from net new guests and which from regulars who just found the brand through the app? Without that split the fee looks fine on the statement and nobody knows whether they are paying it on guests they already owned.
